blocks.text: [II, 614] [col. 68] Chapter 11.
On the Crane.

Belon writes in book 4, chapter 1 of De Avibus that in the anatomy of the crane he observed something peculiar, namely that the windpipe is arranged differently than in other birds. For, adhering to the breastbone, he says, it penetrates the flesh on both sides. And so it is no wonder that its voice is heard so far away. For no bird is as vocal as the crane. Hence Hezekiah, in his song of thanksgiving after he recovered from illness, [col. 69] Es. XXXVIII, 14: כסיס עגור כן אצפצף, like a sis and agor so did I chirp, that is, like a swallow and a crane; of these birds the one has a plaintive voice, the other a most strained one. Between sis and agor the copulative Vau is lacking, as in Hab. III, 11. שמש ירח עמד זבלה, sun, moon (that is, sun and moon) stood still in their place. And 1 Par. II, 1. Reuben, Simeon, Levi, for Reuben, and Simeon, and Levi. Thus Hezekiah's meaning is this: that, afflicted by a grave illness, he not only moaned with a soft murmur like a swallow, but also wailed with a strained voice like a crane. So the Talmudists in tractate Kiddusim, ch. 2, fol. 44a: וצווח דל ככורכיא, And Master Lakish cried out like a crane. And Smyrnaeus [Quintus of Smyrna], in book 3, on the lament of the Nereids at the death of Achilles,
— — — — ταί δ᾽ ἐφέροντο Κλαγγηδὸν κραιπνῇσιν ἐειδόμεναι γεράνοισιν, Ὀσσόμεναι ^{a)} μέγα χεῖμα, — — [tai d᾽ epheronto klangēdon kraipnēsin eeidomenai geranoisin, ossomenai mega cheima]
And they were borne along with clamour, like swift cranes that sense a great storm in advance. And in book 13, on the destruction of Troy,

— — στοναχὴ δὲ δαϊκταμένων αἰζηῶν Ἔπλετο λευγαλέη, περὶ δ᾽ ἴαχε πάντα μέλαθρα [II, 615] Ἄσπετον· οἰμωγὴ δὲ πέλεν στονόεσσα γυναίκων Εἰδομένων γεράνοισιν, ὅτ᾽ αἰετὸν ἀθρήσωσιν. Ὑψόθεν αἴσσοντα δι᾽ αἰθέρος, οὐδ᾽ ἄρα τῇσι Θαρσαλέον στέρνοισι πέλει μένος, ἀλλὰ ἑ μοῦνον Μακρὸν ἀνατρύζουσι, φοβούμεναι ἱερὸν ὄρνιν. [stonachē de daiktamenōn aizēōn epleto leugaleē, peri d᾽ iache panta melathra aspeton; oimōgē de pelen stonoessa gynaikōn eidomenōn geranoisin, hot᾽ aieton athrēsōsin hypsothen aissonta di᾽ aitheros, oud᾽ ara tēsi tharsaleon sternoisi pelei menos, alla he mounon makron anatryzousi, phoboumenai hieron ornin.]

And the groaning of the slain young men was pitiful, and all the houses resounded dreadfully. And most mournful was the wailing of the women, like cranes when they see an eagle swooping from on high through the air. Nor does any brave strength abide in their breast, but they only shriek loudly, dreading the sacred bird of Jove. Homer too, comparing the war-cry of soldiers with the clamour of cranes, at the beginning of book 3 of the Iliad,
Τρῶες μὲν κλαγγῇ τ᾽ ἐνοπῇ τ᾽ ἴσαν ὄρνιθες ὥς, Ἠΰτε περ κλαγγὴ γεράνων πέλει οὐρανόθι πρό. [Trōes men klangē t᾽ enopē t᾽ isan ornithes hōs, ēute per klangē geranōn pelei ouranothi pro.]
The Trojans went with clamour and shouting like birds, as is the clamour of cranes up to heaven. Which Maro imitated in book 10 of the Aeneid,
— — the Dardanians raise a shout to the stars from the walls, as beneath black clouds Strymonian cranes give signals and swim through the air with noise, and flee the South Winds with joyful clamour.
And Martial, to signify that the old woman Philaenis was not only talkative but also loud and Stentorian, in book 9, Epigram 30:

Alas, what a tongue is silent! A thousand auction-blocks could not outdo her, nor the crowd that loves Serapis, nor the curly-haired troop of the morning schoolmaster, nor the bank that resounds with the Strymonian flock.
The following also pertain to the cry of cranes. Homer again, in the place cited above,
Κλαγγῇ ταί γε πέτονται ἐπ᾽ Ὠκεανοῖο ῥοάων, [Klangē tai ge petontai ep᾽ Ōkeanoio rhoaōn,]
With clamour they fly to the streams of Ocean. Hesiod in the Works,
Φράζεσθαι δ᾽ εὖτ᾽ ἂν φωνὴν γεράνου ἐπακούσης, Ὑψόθεν ἐκ νεφέων ἐνιαύσια κεκλαγυίης, [Phrazesthai d᾽ eut᾽ an phōnēn geranou epakousēs, hypsothen ek nepheōn eniausia keklagyiēs,]
Take heed when you hear the voice of the crane crying yearly from on high out of the clouds. Lucretius, book 4, line 18:
As the brief song of the swan is better than that clamour of cranes in the south wind's ethereal scattered clouds.
[II, 616] Claudian, on the Gildonic war,
With huge clamour the cranes leave their summer Thrace, when they exchange the Strymon for the warm Nile.

Accordingly Eustathius calls the crane a φωνητικὴν [phōnētikēn], vocal, bird. And it should be noted that most languages imitate its voice in some way by the very name of the bird. Thus the Hebrew עגור agor, the Chaldee כורכיא kurkeja, the Arabic كركي [kurkī] kurki ^{(1)} and غرنوق [ghurnūq] gurnuk ^{(2)}, the Greek γέρανος [geranos], the Cambro-British garan, the German cran, the Roman grus are so many onomatopoeic words, ὀνοματοποιητικαί [onomatopoiētikai]. Hence Isidore: [col. 70] Cranes took their name from their own voice. For they murmur with such a sound. And gruere [to cry like a crane] is to clamour in the manner of cranes. Festus: Cranes are said gruere, as swine grunnire [grunt]. The little poem De cantu Philomelae:
The crane cries, and in flocks the swans drensant near the rivers.

An old Glossary: Gruunt, γερανίζουσι [geranizousi]. Meanwhile, lest anyone think that cranes always cry with a loud voice, Damir has this about the crane that keeps watch while the others sleep: والذي يحرس يهتف خافي كانه ينذر بانه جارس [wa-lladhī yaḥrusu yahtifu khāfī ka-annahu yundhiru bi-annahu jāris] And the one on guard murmurs only in a low voice, as if it knew that it was on guard. This itself might not unreasonably be referred to the passage of Hezekiah, as though he had joined this soft murmur of the crane with the twittering of the swallow.
